subject: Islamic Studies
q: The first Muslim navy was organised during the caliphate of:
explanation: With Uthman’s permission Muawiyah, governor of Syria, built a fleet that captured Cyprus.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Zat-us-Sawari (Battle of the Masts) was a naval victory over the Byzantines in the caliphate of:
explanation: In about 34 AH the new Muslim fleet defeated the Byzantine navy, ending Byzantine dominance of the eastern Mediterranean.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Hazrat Uthman (RA) was martyred in his house in Madinah in:
explanation: Rebels besieged his house and killed him in 35 AH while he was reciting the Qur’an.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Hazrat Ali (RA) made which city his capital?
explanation: Ali moved the seat of government from Madinah to Kufa in Iraq, which was central to his supporters and to the disturbances he faced.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The Battle of Jamal took place near:
explanation: It was fought near Basra in 36 AH and is named after the camel on which Hazrat Aishah (RA) rode.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The Battle of Siffin was fought between:
explanation: Siffin (37 AH) on the Euphrates ended with a call for arbitration.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The arbitrators appointed after the Battle of Siffin were:
o: Abdullah bin Abbas and Mughirah bin Shu’bah
Abu Musa Ash’ari and Amr bin al-As
Sa’d bin Abi Waqqas and Abdullah bin Umar
explanation: Abu Musa Ash’ari represented Ali’s side and Amr bin al-As represented Muawiyah’s side.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Hazrat Ali (RA) defeated the Kharijites at the Battle of:
explanation: The Kharijites rejected the arbitration and turned to violence; Ali defeated them at Nahrawan in 38 AH.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Hazrat Ali (RA) was martyred in Kufa in 40 AH by:
explanation: Ibn Muljam, a Kharijite, struck him with a poisoned sword as he went to the Fajr prayer.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs lasted about:
explanation: From the death of the Prophet in 11 AH to the end of Ali’s caliphate in 40 AH is about thirty years.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: For most of the Rashidun period, the capital of the Islamic state was:
explanation: Abu Bakr, Umar and Uthman governed from Madinah; Ali later moved to Kufa.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The selection of the four Rightly Guided Caliphs shows that:
o: Each caliph was appointed by the governors
There was no hereditary succession; each was chosen through consultation and pledge
explanation: Abu Bakr was chosen at Saqifah, Umar nominated after consultation, Uthman by a council, and Ali by pledge, but none inherited power.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: On his journey to Jerusalem, Hazrat Umar (RA) took turns with his servant in riding the camel. This shows:
o: Humility and equality between ruler and servant
explanation: Their arriving with the servant on the camel impressed the people of Jerusalem with the caliph’s humility.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Under Hazrat Umar (RA), the governor of a province was generally called:
explanation: The empire was divided into provinces, each under a Wali (governor), with separate officers for justice and revenue.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Who was the first Caliph of Islam?
explanation: Abu Bakr Siddiq was chosen as the first caliph after the death of the Prophet in 11 AH.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The Khilafat-e-Rashidah began in:
explanation: It began with the election of Abu Bakr on the death of the Prophet in 11 AH.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Hazrat Abu Bakr (RA) and Hazrat Umar (RA) are buried:
o: Beside the Holy Prophet (PBUH) in Madinah
explanation: Both lie next to the Prophet in Aishah’s former chamber, now within Masjid-e-Nabawi.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Syria, Iraq, Persia and Egypt were conquered mainly during the caliphate of:
explanation: Umar’s ten-year caliphate saw the defeat of the Byzantines in Syria and Egypt and the collapse of the Sasanian empire.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The Battle of Jamal took place during the caliphate of:
explanation: It was fought in 36 AH, soon after Ali became caliph.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Hazrat Ali (RA) became caliph after the martyrdom of:
explanation: The people of Madinah pledged allegiance to Ali in 35 AH following Uthman’s martyrdom.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Which of the Rightly Guided Caliphs died a natural death?
explanation: Abu Bakr died of illness in 13 AH; the other three caliphs were martyred.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Hazrat Abu Bakr (RA) belonged to which clan of the Quraysh?
explanation: Abu Bakr was from Banu Taym; Umar was from Banu Adi and Uthman from Banu Umayyah.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Hazrat Uthman (RA) belonged to which clan of the Quraysh?
explanation: Uthman bin Affan was a member of Banu Umayyah, the clan of Abu Sufyan and Muawiyah.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The Companions fixed a stipend for Hazrat Abu Bakr (RA) from the Bait-ul-Mal so that he could:
o: Give up trade and devote himself to state affairs
explanation: On the day after his election he set out for the market with cloth to sell; the Companions assigned him a modest allowance instead.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The literal meaning of “Shura” is:
explanation: Shura means mutual consultation; the Qur’an praises believers “whose affairs are decided by consultation among them”.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Which Surah of the Qur’an is named after the principle of consultation?
explanation: Surah Ash-Shura describes the believers as those who conduct their affairs by mutual consultation.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: In the Qur’anic command “obey Allah, obey the Messenger and the Ulul-Amr among you”, Ulul-Amr means:
explanation: Ulul-Amr are those entrusted with authority; obedience to them is subject to obedience to Allah and His Messenger.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The Qur’anic command to “render trusts to those entitled to them” is cited as the basis of:
explanation: Surah An-Nisa links rendering trusts to their rightful holders with judging justly, so public offices must go to the competent and honest.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The Qur’anic phrase “al-qawiyy al-amin” (strong and trustworthy), said about Hazrat Musa (AS), is often cited as the criterion for:
o: Employing a person in a job or office
explanation: The daughter of the old man of Madyan recommended hiring Musa because he was strong and trustworthy: competence plus integrity.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Hazrat Yusuf (AS) asked to be put in charge of the storehouses of Egypt, describing himself as:
explanation: He cited trustworthiness and expertise, the two qualities Islam requires in anyone given public responsibility.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: In the Islamic concept of the state, ultimate sovereignty belongs to:
explanation: Sovereignty belongs to Allah alone; rulers and representatives exercise authority as a trust within the limits He has set.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The Qur’anic idea that man is Allah’s “Khalifah” on earth means that man is:
o: The absolute owner of the earth
Allah’s vicegerent, holding authority as a trust
explanation: As vicegerent, man uses power and resources on Allah’s behalf and is answerable for how he uses them.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: In Islam, a public office is regarded as:
explanation: Office is a trust for which the holder will be accountable before Allah and the people.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: “Bai’ah” in the Islamic political system means:
explanation: Bai’ah is the pledge by which the people accept a ruler’s authority and he accepts obligations towards them.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: In classical Islamic political theory, “Ahl al-Hall wal-Aqd” refers to:
o: Those qualified to choose and advise the ruler on behalf of the community
The judges of the Mazalim courts
The soldiers of the caliph’s guard
explanation: Literally “those who loosen and bind”, they are the representative notables whose consultation and pledge confer authority.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Hisbah was an institution for:
o: Promoting good and preventing wrong in public life, especially in markets
explanation: Hisbah put into practice the duty of enjoining right and forbidding wrong, supervising markets, public morals and services.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The officer in charge of Hisbah was called:
explanation: The Muhtasib inspected markets, weights, prices and public conduct on behalf of the state.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Among the main duties of the Muhtasib was:
o: Checking weights and measures in the markets
explanation: He prevented fraud in trade, such as short weight, adulteration and hoarding, and kept streets and public places in order.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The Ombudsman office in Pakistan (Wafaqi Mohtasib) takes its name from the Islamic institution of:
explanation: Mohtasib is the Urdu form of Muhtasib; the office hears public complaints of maladministration by government agencies.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Hazrat Umar (RA) is reported to have appointed a woman Companion, Hazrat Shifa bint Abdullah (RA), to:
explanation: Shifa bint Abdullah is reported to have been given a role in market supervision, an early example of women in public office.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Mazalim courts in early Islamic administration dealt mainly with:
o: Complaints against officials and the powerful
explanation: Mazalim (grievance) jurisdiction let ordinary people seek redress against governors, officials and influential persons.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Bait-ul-Mal was:
o: The public treasury of the Islamic state
explanation: Bait-ul-Mal held public revenues such as Zakat, Kharaj and Jizyah, kept separate from the ruler’s private wealth.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: In early Islamic administration, the “Shurtah” was the:
explanation: The Shurtah maintained public order and security in the cities.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: In early Islamic administration, the “Barid” was the:
explanation: The Barid carried official correspondence by relays and kept the central government informed about the provinces.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The first person to hold the title of Qazi-ul-Quzat (Chief Justice) was:
explanation: Abu Yusuf, the leading pupil of Abu Hanifa, was made chief judge by the Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Kitab-ul-Kharaj, a treatise on taxation and public finance written for Harun al-Rashid, was the work of:
explanation: Abu Yusuf wrote it at the caliph’s request to set out a just system of land tax and state revenue.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Al-Ahkam al-Sultaniyyah, a classical work on the principles of government, was written by:
explanation: Abu al-Hasan al-Mawardi described the caliphate, ministries, judiciary, Hisbah and Mazalim in this eleventh-century treatise.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Siyasatnama, a book of advice on statecraft, was written by the Seljuk minister:
explanation: Nizam-ul-Mulk, vizier of the Seljuk sultans, wrote it on the duties of rulers and the running of government.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Hazrat Ali’s famous letter of instructions on just governance was addressed to Malik al-Ashtar on his appointment as governor of:
explanation: The letter sets out the duties of a ruler towards all classes of people and is widely cited on good governance.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Hazrat Umar’s well-known letter laying down principles of judicial procedure was addressed to:
explanation: The letter to Abu Musa, then a governor and judge, covers equal treatment of litigants, evidence, settlement and review of judgments.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: In Islamic judicial procedure, the burden of proof lies on:
explanation: The Prophet said evidence is upon the one who makes the claim and the oath upon the one who denies it.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The Holy Prophet (PBUH) instructed that a judge should not decide a case while he is:
explanation: Anger clouds judgment, so a judge must decide only when calm.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The case of Hazrat Ali (RA) over his coat of armour, heard by Qazi Shuraih, is cited as an example of:
o: The caliph appearing in court as an ordinary litigant
explanation: It is reported that the judge decided against the caliph for lack of evidence, and Ali accepted the ruling.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The hadith “Each of you is a shepherd and each of you is responsible for his flock” establishes the principle of:
explanation: From the ruler to the head of a family, everyone entrusted with others will be questioned about them.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The Holy Prophet (PBUH) said that public office should not be given to a person who:
o: Asks for it or covets it
explanation: He said, “We do not appoint to this work anyone who asks for it or is eager for it.”

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The Holy Prophet’s rebuke of the Zakat collector who kept gifts given to him during his duty shows that such gifts are:
o: Not lawful for the official to keep
Lawful up to a small amount
explanation: He asked whether the official would have received those gifts had he stayed at home; gifts due to office belong to the public.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: In Islamic teaching, “Ghulul” refers to:
o: Misappropriation of public property or spoils
explanation: The Qur’an warns that whoever misappropriates will bring what he took on the Day of Judgment.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The Holy Prophet (PBUH) cursed both the giver and the taker of:
explanation: Rishwat corrupts justice and administration, so both parties to a bribe are condemned.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: According to the teaching “there is no obedience to a creature in disobedience of the Creator”, the ruler must be obeyed:
o: Only in what is right and lawful
explanation: Obedience to authority is binding only within what Allah permits; an order to sin is not to be obeyed.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: When a man publicly questioned Hazrat Umar (RA) about the extra cloth in his garment, the incident illustrated:
o: The ruler’s accountability to the people
explanation: Umar did not rebuke him but had his son explain that he had given his own share, showing that the ruler answers to the public.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Hazrat Umar (RA) went on night rounds in Madinah mainly to:
o: Learn the real condition of the people
explanation: His patrols helped him discover hardship, such as a mother boiling stones to comfort hungry children, and relieve it himself.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: To prevent corruption, Hazrat Umar (RA) required his governors to:
o: Hand over their homes to the state
Have their assets recorded on appointment
explanation: Their wealth was recorded when they took office, and unexplained increases were questioned and confiscated for the treasury.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Hazrat Umar’s saying that he would be answerable even for a dog dying of hunger by the Euphrates reflects:
o: Kindness to animals as a law of trade
The ruler’s responsibility for public welfare
explanation: He regarded the welfare of every living being in his domain as his responsibility before Allah.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Hazrat Umar (RA) compared his position with regard to public funds to that of:
o: A guardian of an orphan’s property
explanation: He took from the treasury only what was reasonable for his needs, as a guardian may from an orphan’s wealth.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Hazrat Umar (RA) allowed his son Abdullah to attend the electoral council only as an adviser, without the right to be chosen, in order to avoid:
explanation: He excluded his own son from candidacy to keep the caliphate free from family succession.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Hazrat Umar’s rebuke of the governor’s son who struck an Egyptian Copt (“since when have you enslaved people whom their mothers bore free?”) illustrates:
o: Equality of all citizens before the law
The rights of the Muslim army
explanation: The report is cited to show that even a governor’s family was not above the law and that non-Muslim citizens had equal rights to justice.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: When sending Hazrat Mu’adh (RA) and Hazrat Abu Musa (RA) to Yemen, the Holy Prophet (PBUH) instructed them to:
o: Make things easy and not difficult
explanation: He told them to make things easy, give good news, not drive people away, and to cooperate with each other.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The Holy Prophet (PBUH) administered distant regions such as Yemen and Bahrain by:
o: Appointing governors and Zakat collectors answerable to him
explanation: He sent Amils and governors, instructed them in their duties and checked their accounts on return.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: In the Islamic system, a “Qazi” is a:
explanation: The Qazi decides disputes according to the Shariah; judicial independence was stressed from the Rashidun period.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The Arabic word “Wazir” means:
explanation: The Wazir assisted the ruler in running the government; the office became prominent under the Abbasids.
